variants.title: Run the benchmark
variants.context: A defensible code benchmark run has four stages: freeze the manifest, sample candidates, contain execution, then score and retain evidence. Each stage records enough detail to reproduce both the number and every exclusion.
variants.prompt: A team wants to compare two model builds on HumanEval and publish the result. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Score and retain evidence: run public and protected tests, compute the declared pass@k estimator, then report slices, uncertainty, cost, and exclusions.
Sample candidates: keep every completion, seed, token count, model revision, and candidate index, without silently resampling failures.
Contain execution: run each candidate in a disposable isolated environment with no ambient credentials and bounded CPU, memory, files, processes, and network.
Freeze the manifest: version the task revision, prompt, entry point, runtime image, dependencies, hidden-test policy, decoding settings, and timeout.

variants.hint: Which stage has to be settled before a single token is generated?
variants.explanation: The manifest is frozen first so the score is reproducible; scoring comes last because it depends on contained execution.

variants.title: Run the benchmark
variants.context: A defensible code benchmark run has four stages: freeze the manifest, sample candidates, contain execution, then score and retain evidence. Each stage records enough detail to reproduce both the number and every exclusion.
variants.prompt: An evaluator crashes partway through a run and the team restarts it. Put the stages in order so the rerun reproduces the original number.

items.text: Recompute pass@k from the per-candidate outcomes and compare slices, denominators, and exclusions against the original report.
Regenerate candidates under the recorded seed policy and candidate count, keeping every completion rather than the best-looking one.
Reload the frozen manifest with the same benchmark revision, prompt template, decoding settings, and timeout as the original run.
Execute each candidate again inside the pinned runtime image with the same package allowlist and resource limits.

variants.hint: Reproduction replays the same contracts in the same order.
variants.explanation: A rerun is only evidence when it replays the frozen manifest; anything regenerated under new settings is a different experiment.

variants.title: Run the benchmark
variants.context: A defensible code benchmark run has four stages: freeze the manifest, sample candidates, contain execution, then score and retain evidence. Each stage records enough detail to reproduce both the number and every exclusion.
variants.prompt: A coding assistant is a release candidate. Put the run in order, ending with the exposure decision.

items.text: Score public and protected tests separately and publish pass@1 with denominators and uncertainty.
Grant the build that beats the baseline a bounded canary path rather than an unrestricted deployment.
Freeze the task, generation, execution, and scoring contracts before any sampling begins.
Sample the declared number of candidates per task from the pinned model build.
Run each candidate in the disposable sandbox and record exit reason, resource use, and redacted failure class.

variants.hint: Offline evidence earns exposure; it does not replace it.
variants.explanation: Offline pass@k earns controlled exposure behind a baseline and a bounded canary, never an unrestricted rollout.

variants.title: Fail closed on a bad run
variants.context: When the verifier cannot support the claim, the run fails closed. Timeouts are classified as failures, a flaky verifier holds the release, contaminated tasks are quarantined, and malicious behavior blocks release instead of becoming a retry.
variants.prompt: A candidate opens a socket to an external host from inside the sandbox. Put the response in order.

items.text: Investigate the isolation failure instead of turning the same run into a retry.
Preserve the minimal forensic record of the attempt.
Block the release for this run.
Rotate any secret that could have been exposed.

variants.hint: Containment comes before curiosity, and neither is a retry.
variants.explanation: Policy-violating behavior blocks release, preserves minimal forensics, rotates exposed secrets, and triggers an isolation investigation.

variants.title: Fail closed on a bad run
variants.context: When the verifier cannot support the claim, the run fails closed. Timeouts are classified as failures, a flaky verifier holds the release, contaminated tasks are quarantined, and malicious behavior blocks release instead of becoming a retry.
variants.prompt: One task slice shows ten percent of candidates exceeding the wall-clock timeout. Put the response in order.

items.text: Terminate the isolated workload rather than letting it retry indefinitely.
Classify each timed-out candidate as a failure rather than a missing result.
Report the timeout rate broken down by task slice.
Capture bounded logs from the run instead of unbounded output.

variants.hint: A timeout is an outcome, not an absence of one.
variants.explanation: Timeouts count as failures with bounded logs and a terminated workload, and the timeout rate is reported per slice.

variants.title: Fail closed on a bad run
variants.context: When the verifier cannot support the claim, the run fails closed. Timeouts are classified as failures, a flaky verifier holds the release, contaminated tasks are quarantined, and malicious behavior blocks release instead of becoming a retry.
variants.prompt: The protected suite passes and fails on the same candidate across reruns. Put the response in order.

items.text: Hold the release, because a non-deterministic verifier produces weak evidence.
Repair or replace the harness before it is used as a release gate again.
Rerun the harness on known-good fixtures to see whether the verifier itself is unstable.
Rerun it on known-bad fixtures to confirm it still detects real failures.

variants.hint: Suspect the instrument before you blame the candidate.
variants.explanation: Flakiness is diagnosed against known-good and known-bad fixtures first, and an unstable verifier holds the release.

variants.title: Estimate pass@k
variants.context: For a task with n sampled candidates of which c pass every test, pass@k estimates the chance that a uniformly chosen set of k candidates contains at least one passing solution. The unbiased estimator is 1 minus C(n minus c, k) divided by C(n, k).
variants.prompt: A task is sampled 6 times and 3 of the 6 candidates pass every test. Report pass@2 as a percentage.
variants.hint: Count the pairs that contain no passing candidate, then take the complement.
variants.explanation: C(3,2) of the C(6,2) pairs are all-failing, so 1 minus 3 over 15 is 0.8, or 80 percent.

mistakes.feedback: That is c divided by n, the pass@1 rate, not the chance that either of two draws passes.
That is the all-failing fraction C(n minus c, k) over C(n, k); pass@k is one minus that.

variants.title: Estimate pass@k
variants.context: For a task with n sampled candidates of which c pass every test, pass@k estimates the chance that a uniformly chosen set of k candidates contains at least one passing solution. The unbiased estimator is 1 minus C(n minus c, k) divided by C(n, k).
variants.prompt: A task is sampled 5 times and 2 of the 5 candidates pass every test. Report pass@2 as a percentage.
variants.hint: How many two-candidate sets can be built entirely from the failing candidates?
variants.explanation: C(3,2) of the C(5,2) pairs are all-failing, so 1 minus 3 over 10 is 0.7, or 70 percent.

mistakes.feedback: That is c divided by n, the pass@1 rate; sampling twice raises the chance of at least one pass.
That is the all-failing fraction; subtract it from 1 to get pass@k.

variants.title: Estimate pass@k
variants.context: For a task with n sampled candidates of which c pass every test, pass@k estimates the chance that a uniformly chosen set of k candidates contains at least one passing solution. The unbiased estimator is 1 minus C(n minus c, k) divided by C(n, k).
variants.prompt: A task is sampled 5 times and only 1 of the 5 candidates passes every test. Report pass@3 as a percentage.
variants.hint: Build the triples from the failing candidates only, then take the complement.
variants.explanation: C(4,3) of the C(5,3) triples are all-failing, so 1 minus 4 over 10 is 0.6, or 60 percent.

mistakes.feedback: That is c divided by n, the pass@1 rate, not the chance that one of three draws passes.
That is the all-failing fraction C(4,3) over C(5,3); pass@k is one minus that.

variants.title: Bound the claim
variants.context: A pass@k number supports a claim only inside its declared protocol. Contamination, incomplete behavioral coverage, the single-language function-level task shape, and sampling sensitivity each narrow what the score can certify.
variants.prompt: A crawl finds that 22 of the 164 HumanEval tasks appear near-verbatim in the tuning corpus. What should the report do?
options: Quarantine the exposed cluster, rescore on the remaining tasks, and disclose the finding.
Keep the tasks in the denominator, since near-duplicates are not exact matches.
Drop HumanEval entirely and report only the MBPP score for this build.
optionFeedback: Correct: exposed and near-duplicate tasks are quarantined, the score is recomputed, and the contamination is disclosed.
A near-duplicate is still exposure, so those tasks are no longer an independent holdout.
MBPP is public too, so swapping benchmarks hides the problem instead of measuring it.
variants.hint: What word can you no longer use for an exposed task?
variants.explanation: Contamination is measured and disclosed, and exposed tasks lose the status of an independent holdout.

variants.title: Bound the claim
variants.context: A pass@k number supports a claim only inside its declared protocol. Contamination, incomplete behavioral coverage, the single-language function-level task shape, and sampling sensitivity each narrow what the score can certify.
variants.prompt: A single-suggestion completion feature scores pass@1 of 0.41 and pass@10 of 0.78. Marketing wants to publish 0.78. What is the honest move?
options: Publish the average of the two numbers so both views are represented.
Publish pass@1 as the feature metric and pass@10 only with the search budget it implies.
Publish pass@10, since the model can demonstrably produce a passing program.
optionFeedback: Averaging two different protocols produces a number that answers no question at all.
Correct: pass@1 matches a feature that offers one suggestion, and pass@10 must carry its ranking and discard cost.
The feature never shows ten candidates, so pass@10 describes a product that does not exist yet.
variants.hint: Which number describes the thing the user actually sees?
variants.explanation: pass@k measures an assisted search budget, so it is reported with that budget rather than as a drop-in replacement for pass@1.

variants.title: Bound the claim
variants.context: A pass@k number supports a claim only inside its declared protocol. Contamination, incomplete behavioral coverage, the single-language function-level task shape, and sampling sensitivity each narrow what the score can certify.
variants.prompt: The evaluator runs each candidate as a subprocess with a timeout on the CI host, using the checked-out repository and the package-manager token. What is the standing of the result?
options: The number may be arithmetically right, but the run is not a valid release result.
The timeout bounds the damage, so the measured score still stands as a gate.
The result is valid because no candidate in this run actually misbehaved.
optionFeedback: Correct: a correct number from an unsafe evaluator is not a valid release result.
A subprocess with a timeout is not an isolation boundary; it bounds time, not access.
Absence of observed misbehavior in one run says nothing about the boundary that was never there.
variants.hint: Ask what the candidate could have reached, not what it did reach.
variants.explanation: Generated code is an untrusted workload, so ambient credentials, a repository checkout, or host access invalidate the run regardless of the score.

variants.title: Sort the run manifest
variants.context: The run manifest holds four contracts. The task contract fixes what is asked, the generation contract fixes how candidates are produced, the execution contract fixes where they run, and the scoring contract fixes how the number is computed.
variants.prompt: A reviewer asks what each part of the manifest pins down. Match each contract to what it fixes.

pairs.label: Task contract
pairs.detail: Benchmark revision, task IDs, prompt template, function signature, allowed imports, and public versus protected test identity.

pairs.label: Generation contract
pairs.detail: Model build, temperature, top-p, maximum tokens, seed policy, candidates per task, and any repair loop.

pairs.label: Execution contract
pairs.detail: Runtime image digest, package allowlist, CPU and memory limits, wall-clock timeout, filesystem policy, and network policy.

pairs.label: Scoring contract
pairs.detail: Whether every test must pass, the pass@k values, aggregation weights, dropped-task policy, and interval method.

variants.hint: Ask whether the field describes what is asked, how it is produced, where it runs, or how it is counted.
variants.explanation: Four separate contracts keep the reproduction argument auditable: change one and you know exactly which claim moved.

variants.title: Sort the run manifest
variants.context: The run manifest holds four contracts. The task contract fixes what is asked, the generation contract fixes how candidates are produced, the execution contract fixes where they run, and the scoring contract fixes how the number is computed.
variants.prompt: Four questions arrive during a release review. Match each question to the contract that answers it.

pairs.label: Why did this task's score change after a library upgrade?
pairs.detail: Execution contract: the runtime image digest and the package allowlist.

pairs.label: Was the passing answer the first suggestion or the sixth?
pairs.detail: Generation contract: candidates per task and the recorded candidate index.

pairs.label: Is this task still an independent holdout?
pairs.detail: Task contract: the benchmark revision and the protected test identity.

pairs.label: Why is the denominator 158 instead of 164?

variants.hint: Trace the question back to the stage that could have moved the answer.
variants.explanation: Each review question resolves to exactly one contract, which is why the manifest is split rather than kept as one blob.

variants.title: Sort the run manifest
variants.context: The run manifest holds four contracts. The task contract fixes what is asked, the generation contract fixes how candidates are produced, the execution contract fixes where they run, and the scoring contract fixes how the number is computed.
variants.prompt: A manifest is missing several fields. Match each omission to the failure it causes.

pairs.label: No runtime image digest
pairs.detail: Reruns can silently change the dependency versions the candidate is compiled and tested against.

pairs.label: No seed policy or candidate index
pairs.detail: Nobody can tell whether a passing answer was the first sample or the tenth.

pairs.label: No dropped-task policy
pairs.detail: The denominator can move between runs without anyone noticing.

pairs.label: No protected test identity
pairs.detail: Fitting the visible examples becomes indistinguishable from generalizing.

variants.hint: Each missing field breaks one specific part of the reproduction story.
variants.explanation: A missing manifest field does not just lose detail; it removes the ability to say which stage caused a change in the number.
